This concludes the twelfth chapter, the Examination of Suffering.

To this, it is said: "Even if those four modes do not exist, suffering and external things, the conditioned phenomena <note>original: <term>saṃskāra</term></note>, do exist." To this, it is explained:

Whatever phenomena are deceptive are false,
So the Blessed One has said.
All conditioned phenomena are deceptive,
Therefore, they are false.

Regarding this, the Blessed One said in the sūtras: "Whatever phenomena are deceptive are false. Monks, it is like this: Nirvana, the non-deceptive phenomenon, is the supreme truth." Because of this, since all conditioned phenomena are deceptive, they are false. Because they appear mistakenly, their imagined essence is empty. To this, it is said: "If whatever conditioned phenomena are deceptive are false, then since both are similar in meaning to non-existence, how can the deceptive nature establish falsehood?" To this, it is explained:

If whatever is deceptive
Is false, what is there to be deceived?
The Blessed One said this
To fully demonstrate emptiness.

If it is said that whatever is deceptive is false, and they are similar in meaning to non-existence, then what would be deceived? Deception is a mistaken appearance, while falsehood refers to the emptiness of the imagined essence; since this is not the same as total non-existence, it is appropriate to establish falsehood through deceptive phenomena. Therefore, one should understand that when the Blessed One spoke of "deceptive phenomena," he was fully demonstrating emptiness. To this, it is said:

Things lack inherent existence,
Because change is seen.

When the Blessed One spoke of "falsehood," it did not mean non-existence or the selflessness of phenomena; rather, it meant that things lack an inherent nature <note>original: <term>svabhāva</term></note> in terms of a person. Why? Because we see things

old_translation:
Not only do those four modes not exist, but external things such as form and so forth also do not exist in those four modes.

### Examination of Suffering
#### The Twelfth Chapter

It is said here: Even if those four modes do not exist, suffering and external entities, the <term>samskaras</term> <gloss>conditioned phenomena</gloss>, do exist.

To this, it is explained:

Whatever phenomena are deceptive are false,
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
All conditioned phenomena are deceptive phenomena,
Therefore, they are false.

In this regard, the Blessed One said in the <term>sutras</term> <gloss>scriptural discourses</gloss>: "Whatever phenomenon is deceptive, that is false. O monks, it is like this: Nirvana, the non-deceptive phenomenon, is the supreme truth." Because of this, since all conditioned phenomena are deceptive phenomena, they are false. Because they appear erroneously, they are empty of any conceptualized essence.

It is said here: If whatever is a deceptive phenomenon is false, and both of those are the same in meaning as being non-existent, then how can falsity be established by deceptive phenomena?

To this, it is explained:

If whatever is a deceptive phenomenon
Is false, what is it that deceives?
That which was spoken by the Blessed One
Completely demonstrates emptiness.

If what was spoken of as "deceptive phenomena" is false, and that is the same as the meaning of non-existence, then what could possibly be deceived? In this way, deception is an erroneous appearance, while "false" means being empty of a conceptualized inherent nature. Since it is not the same as mere non-existence, it is appropriate to establish falsity through deceptive phenomena. Therefore, one should understand that what the Blessed One spoke of as "deceptive phenomena" serves to completely demonstrate emptiness.

It is said here:

Entities have no inherent nature,
Because change is observed.

When the Blessed One spoke of "falsity," it did not mean non-existence or the absence of a self in phenomena, but rather that entities lack a personal inherent nature. Why is this? Because change into other states is observed.

<summary>This page concludes the examination of suffering and begins the thirteenth chapter's analysis of conditioned phenomena. It argues that all conditioned things are deceptive and false because they lack inherent nature and are subject to change.</summary>
